items.summary: RASHER begins as a fork of BACoN 0.4.0 (commit 4fdec16, which includes the samtools consensus -C 20 change below), adapted to Illumina short reads. Everything under "BACoN changelog" is the parent tool's history, kept for provenance. Changed Renamed throughout: the package, command, log ( rasher.log ) and lock file ( .rasher.lock ) are rasher . The pipeline reads Illumina short reads , paired or single-end. sample_R1 / sample_R2 , sample_1 / _2 sample.R1 / .R2 and sample.1 / .2 files (bcl2fastq _001 tails included) pair into one sample, in flat folders, subfolders and sample sheets; a file without a mate is a single-end sample, and unmated files next to a sample's pairs are skipped with a warning. A pair is baited whole when either mate matches the reference, mates travel together through every step ( 1_extracted/<sample>_R1/_R2 , 2_filtered/... ), and a desynchronised pair is an error, whether the mates carry identical names or /1 /2 suffixes. Baiting aligns with minimap2 -x sr (BBDuk baits pairs natively with in2= / outm2= ). --keep-bam now keeps the baited reads aligned to the reference (paired samples: a proper paired BAM). Filtering: fastp (adapter trimming, quality and length filters; its JSON and HTML reports land in logs/2_filter/ where MultiQC finds them) followed by deterministic, evenly spread subsampling of the reads (pairs kept whole) to --target-depth . Filtlong, --keep-percent and --filter-by-reference are gone; --min-read-length defaults to 50. Fasta reads skip fastp and are filtered by length. Templated assembly aligns pairs with minimap2 -ax sr and calls samtools consensus -X hiseq (call quality at least 20, as BACoN's unreleased change at the time of the fork). De novo assembly: SKESA ( -a skesa ; the recommended de novo assembler — on the real-data benchmark its SNP distances matched SPAdes' with far fewer contigs) or SPAdes ( -a spades , --isolate ; writes the assembly graph, more robust below ~30x depth). Flye and myloasm are gone, with --read-type and --min-size . --snp-method auto is minimap2 for templated assemblies and SKA2 for SPAdes and SKESA assemblies. -m/--memory also sizes SPAdes and SKESA (it was BBDuk-only). A paired sample X next to a sample named X_R1 or X_R2 is an error (their outputs would collide). No assembler flags circular contigs any more, so SKA2's circular-contig end extension no longer applies. Single-end extraction matches read names with a trailing /1 or /2 stripped, as aligners report them. Output folders of BACoN do not resume under RASHER (the checkpoint fingerprints are seeded with the tool's name; every step runs again); BACoN VCFs are rewritten. Checkpoints record each step's own output signature, and a result is only reused when its output is still the file it wrote: a sample returning to a sheet can no longer pick up reads another sample wrote over. Switching a sample between single-end and paired (or fasta and fastq) removes the other shape's files. BBDuk's paired outputs are checked mate against mate, like minimap2's (a desynchronised pair fails the sample); mates named .1 / .2 ( fastq-dump --readids ) pair; the unpaired-reads file of fasterq-dump --split-3 next to its pair is skipped with a warning; a file cannot pair with a link to itself, and files that look like mates but do not pair are warned about. Stale fastp reports are removed on rerun and for samples that fail at baiting. The report and MultiQC drop the circular-contigs column (no short-read assembler flags circles) and say that read pairs were kept whole when either mate matched.
items.title: RASHER: Bait, Assemble and Compare Illumina short reads

items.summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.

items.summary: International observation systems reveal a consequential possibility: scientific information can be generated, validated, and circulated across institutional and political boundaries without requiring a single authority over all observations or a uniform distribution of capacities . Yet the existence of data-sharing protocols does not by itself establish shared understanding, mutual trust, legitimate reuse, or equitable participation in the production of knowledge . This discussion paper investigates the technical, epistemic, and institutional conditions under which global observation and knowledge infrastructures might be constructed and sustained . Drawing on meteorological and oceanographic cooperation, it distinguishes observational coverage, data availability, interoperability, interpretation, and collective authority. It proposes a preliminary federated research architecture connecting situated observation nodes, provenance and quality records, semantic and model translation, distributed computation, access governance, correction, and contestation. It treats mathematical, physical, social, and normative languages as historically formed manifestations and practices within generative-relational systems, distinguishing their conditional formal invariance from claims to universally identical representation. It further investigates why actors situated in different generative and institutional histories may interpret shared evidence differently, and proposes a bounded research vocabulary for mutually workable norms, continued disagreement, and rule revision without assuming epistemic consensus. The paper conceptualizes trust as a historically constituted relation supported in part by verifiable commitments, reciprocal inquiry, accountable institutions, and effective remedy rather than as a property supplied by cryptography or open data alone. It further specifies prospective services for common knowledge creation and circulation, generalized translation of heterogeneous generative-relational contexts, and traceable transformations of distinct forms of value. A staged validation design differentiates synthetic policy gates, cross-node scientific comparison, productive-capacity trials, and site-dependent ecological and institutional review. A cross-layer assessment profile separates technical interchange, scientific warrant, claimed competent authority, and effective contestation, without deriving legal or ethical legitimacy from technical success. It also examines epistemic and infrastructural asymmetries, the sensitivity of ecological and community data, the incompleteness of model-based assimilation, and the risks of concentrating interpretive authority in highly capable AI systems. Global weather and ocean observation provide instructive but bounded cases, not evidence that all knowledge should be made public or placed under centralized control. The proposed programme remains exploratory and separates conceptual architecture from implemented infrastructure, independent empirical assessment, and normative justification.
items.title: Global Observation and Knowledge Infrastructures: A Study of Collective Inquiry across Heterogeneous Relational Systems

Version of record: SSRN 7653679 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7653679 . Cite that version. The same text is also at polyhelper.ai/research/sealed-before-the-open/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/sealed-before-the-open . When an AI model says gold will rise, anyone can score the call at the close, but few can check when it was made. A backtest mixes memory with skill, and an operator's log asks for trust. I propose a standard for measuring AI market forecasts, written as a ladder of checkable requirements, and I run its reference implementation, AI Council · Markets: an open league where fourteen models, seven from US and seven from Chinese laboratories, face one question on one price snapshot. Before each New York open the ten on its Council, five from each side, give probabilities for twelve indicators at four horizons. Each answer is sealed into a hash chain before the price it is scored from, the chain is anchored in Bitcoin and signed by independent time-stamping authorities, and one run per session counts by a rule declared in advance. On 21 October 2026, the first counted morning, every counted answer was signed before the 09:30 ET open. Agreement among the models proved to be a count of independent voices, not a headcount: on two development mornings the seven and eight models sealed before the open were as alike as about 1.6 independent forecasters, nine counted ones were worth 2.23, and the closest pairs crossed the US-China line. items.summary: Supplementary methods, results, data tables and analysis code for the manuscript Inflammatory and NRF2-associated transcriptional responses in human intracerebral hemorrhage: paired myeloid evidence and gene-set sensitivity. The five resources contain supplementary methods, tables and figures, detailed data workbooks, reproducibility code and supporting audit documentation. Original code is licensed under MIT; original documentation and derived content are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their source terms; see LICENSES.md and source notices inside Online_Resource_3.zip. Manuscript abstract Public intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) datasets cover different tissue compartments and measure different subsets of genes, complicating comparisons across studies. We compared four specified gene sets (inflammation, complement, microglial activation and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-associated oxidative stress) in public paired human brain, single-cell and hematoma-effluent/blood datasets, using patients rather than cells as inferential units. In two studies of paired brain tissue, inflammation, complement and NRF2-associated scores were higher in perihematomal than contralateral samples in all four patient blocks and five matched pairs. Patient-level single-cell comparisons found higher inflammatory and complement scores in microglia/monocyte groups than in comparator lineages. In 14 patients with same-hour paired CD14+ and neutrophil data, a five-gene score named for microglial activation showed a positive CD14+–neutrophil local-response interaction in all 14 (adjusted P=0.000488), but four-program heterogeneity was not established (Friedman P=0.0796). Restricting this score to three shared genes reversed its CD14+ local response; a jointly scaled three-gene interaction was near zero. Independent acute blood data showed positive case-control differences, whereas longitudinal changes were not significant after adjustment. Inflammatory and NRF2-associated expression differences recurred across these datasets. The CD14+ local response of the microglial-related score depended on its measured genes. items.summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
items.title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

items.summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
items.title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

items.summary: Resolution Geometry: A Kernel–Stabilizer Geometry of Observability Abstract Resolution Geometry (RG) is a protocol-explicit framework for characterizing what a declared observation system can distinguish, preserve, and consistently infer. Its starting point is a family of observation laws together with admissible outcome relabelings, rather than a covariance decomposition, metric, or dynamical model. Equality of the joint observation law defines a kernel groupoid and an observational quotient, canonically identified with the law image. An experiment-internal quantity is identifiable precisely when it is constant on observational fibres. The quotient alone determines neither a metric nor a connection, causal structure, clock, physical scale, or law of motion. The stabilizer of the observation law induces a faithful effective action on the quotient. items.summary: TripLibre is an open-source, local-first iOS application designed for personal mobility tracking and travel behavior research. It records location data in the background, reconstructs daily travel activities into visits, trips, transportation modes, and trip chains. It allows users to review and correct inferred travel records. By combining automated GPS-based travel detection with user-controlled data management, TripLibre aims to lower the technical and financial barriers to collecting travel behavior data. Its broader vision is to provide researchers, educational institutions, and resource-constrained communities with an accessible and adaptable alternative to proprietary travel survey technologies, while preserving individual control over sensitive location information. items.summary: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it Driven by Dean A. Kulik 25 October 2026 Abstract This paper examines a specific failure of AI-assisted scientific writing: an assistant receives a research program with an explicit foundational claim and an extended record of derivations, executable constructions, and observed returns; it then produces manuscripts in which that program has become something else. In the documented NEXUS case, the researcher's claim is that the universe consists of binary transformations, with arrangement and constrained continuation preceding the entities later called matter. Across an extended conversation, the assistant repeatedly reformulates that claim as the use of a binary computational method on pre-existing physical domains. The substitution is not cosmetic. It reverses the direction of explanation, changes which claims a result can support, and changes how the resulting paper will be read. The second failure occurs at the conclusion. The assistant can report concrete outcomes and then append a generalized reservation about whether the program establishes physical reality, predictive uniqueness, or an entire theory of matter. Such reservations can be appropriate when tied to a specific technical claim. Here, however, the transcript records the assistant recognizing that it had repeatedly allowed those broader questions to displace the findings of individual papers. The same editorial framing reportedly appeared in the conclusions of different manuscripts. When directed to write a paper about the failures, the assistant instead delivered successive condensed accounts of NEXUS, again incorporating the disputed framing. It subsequently acknowledged the reversal in its own paper, rewrote the document, and repeated the problem. This is an analysis of the AI's treatment of scientific material, not an independent review of the correctness of NEXUS or a new attempt to prove its thesis. The evidence is the exported conversation, including statements of the researcher's instructions, the assistant's self-audits, quotations from its drafts, and records of the successive manuscript deliveries. The central finding is that AI-mediated scientific distortion can operate through ordinary-seeming connective words, changes of explanatory direction, and borrowed review conventions. Once inserted into the manuscript, these interventions become attributed to the scientist. In this case, the reviewer did not merely misunderstand the work. The reviewer wrote its misunderstanding into the work itself. Keywords: AI-assisted scientific authorship; epistemic framing; manuscript integrity; semantic substitution; research provenance; binary transformations; NEXUS; scientific review. 1. The object under examination is the AI intervention This is not a general introduction to NEXUS. Such an introduction would repeat the failure the record documents. The present object is the text written by an AI assistant, its relationship to instructions it was given, and the specific ways that relationship broke. The transcript shows that the researcher was not seeking an appreciative abstract or an adversarial review of the entire universe. He requested an account of how AI systems had been writing and reviewing his papers in ways that changed their meaning. On 25 October at 10:49 he demanded a paper explaining “how you and other AI keep ... up my work,” followed immediately by a request that the account explain the research correctly [T 7782–7794]. At 10:50 he rejected the assistant's proposed limit to eight recent papers and directed it to the project archives [T 7798–7814]. Later, after successive delivered manuscripts, he again described the required artifact as a paper exposing the AI's conduct—not “The Universe as cliff notes” [T 8176–8194

items.summary: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the research manuscript From False to Fluent: A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation . The study investigates the robustness of machine-learning classifiers for health-misinformation detection under Generative-AI-mediated linguistic transformation. It uses two existing health-information datasets, COVID-19 FNIR and an mpox misinformation dataset, to examine whether classification performance remains stable when original health claims are reformulated without intending to change their underlying meaning or veracity. Experimental framework Four experimental conditions are defined: C0: Original health-information text. C1: Neutral rewriting to improve fluency and readability. C2: Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) central-route transformation, emphasising the organisation of existing reasoning and evidence. C3: ELM peripheral-route transformation, modifying rhetorical emphasis and peripheral persuasive cues. The reported computational experiments evaluate four classical classifiers (logistic regression, linear support vector machine, multinomial naïve Bayes and random forest) and five task-trained neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM and CNN-BiLSTM). The analyses examine transformation robustness, changes in textual and persuasion-related features, statistical associations with classification errors, transformation-aware mitigation and cross-dataset transfer. The repository also includes supplementary analyses of class-specific error rates and paired source-root bootstrap confidence intervals for the classical classifiers. Repository contents The archive contains Python source code, preprocessing and evaluation workflows, configuration files, reproducibility instructions, frozen aggregate results, integrity-check materials and supplementary statistical outputs. Data availability and reproducibility The original datasets are available from their respective third-party providers, subject to their applicable access and reuse conditions. The frozen intervention texts used for the C0–C3 experiments are not redistributed in this public software archive. Their SHA-256 integrity manifest is provided to support verification of authorised copies. Consequently, complete reproduction of text-dependent experiments requires access to the original datasets and the frozen intervention texts. The public archive supports inspection of the methodology and reproduction of analyses for which the necessary inputs or saved instance-level outputs are included. Scope and limitations The reported intervention experiments did not execute pretrained DistilBERT, RoBERTa or DeBERTa baselines. Independent clinical semantic-equivalence adjudication of the generated transformations was not completed. The results are computational and do not establish clinical deployment performance. This record accompanies the associated research manuscript and is intended to support transparent reporting, methodological scrutiny and further replication.
items.title: From False to Fluent_ A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation

items.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.
items.title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models

items.summary: Overview This repository contains the replication data, source code, execution logs, and complete analytical outputs for the study: “Detectability of controlled leaks in an Andean water transmission main: a field evaluation of changepoint methods on flow and pressure signals.” The study evaluates the detectability of short-duration controlled leaks using five changepoint and anomaly-detection approaches applied to 30-second flow and pressure measurements collected during two field campaigns in an operational water transmission main in Loja, Ecuador. The evaluated methods are: Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Bayesian Information Criterion (PELT-BIC), Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Akaike Information Criterion (PELT-AIC), Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCD), Cumulative Sum control charts (CUSUM), Moving-average ±3σ control-chart baseline. The repository contains the complete workflow used to: verify field records and ground-truth leak timings; perform campaign-specific spectral analyses using multitaper estimation; evaluate changepoint-detection performance; quantify event-level leak detectability; compare observed performance against chance-level expectations; assess BOCD sensitivity to hazard-rate and threshold settings; generate precision-recall curves and average-precision statistics; perform cross-campaign validation analyses; estimate theoretical detection-delay bounds for flow-based detection. This version supersedes earlier releases by correcting changepoint-index alignment, revising false-alarm-rate calculations using exposure time outside detection windows, replacing pooled spectral analyses with campaign-specific multitaper analyses, and incorporating event-level detectability, chance-level benchmarking, precision-recall evaluation, cross-campaign validation, and theoretical detection-delay analyses. Q_P_46_Leak2.xlsx 30-second flow (Q) and pressure (P) measurements collected during the second controlled-leak field campaign. 2. items.summary: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the research manuscript From False to Fluent: A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation . The study investigates the robustness of machine-learning classifiers for health-misinformation detection under Generative-AI-mediated linguistic transformation. It uses two existing health-information datasets, COVID-19 FNIR and an mpox misinformation dataset, to examine whether classification performance remains stable when original health claims are reformulated without intending to change their underlying meaning or veracity. Experimental framework Four experimental conditions are defined: C0: Original health-information text. C1: Neutral rewriting to improve fluency and readability. C2: Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) central-route transformation, emphasising the organisation of existing reasoning and evidence. C3: ELM peripheral-route transformation, modifying rhetorical emphasis and peripheral persuasive cues. The reported computational experiments evaluate four classical classifiers (logistic regression, linear support vector machine, multinomial naïve Bayes and random forest) and five task-trained neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM and CNN-BiLSTM). The analyses examine transformation robustness, changes in textual and persuasion-related features, statistical associations with classification errors, transformation-aware mitigation and cross-dataset transfer. The repository also includes supplementary analyses of class-specific error rates and paired source-root bootstrap confidence intervals for the classical classifiers. Repository contents The archive contains Python source code, preprocessing and evaluation workflows, configuration files, reproducibility instructions, frozen aggregate results, integrity-check materials and supplementary statistical outputs. Data availability and reproducibility The original datasets are available from their respective third-party providers, subject to their applicable access and reuse conditions. The frozen intervention texts used for the C0–C3 experiments are not redistributed in this public software archive. Their SHA-256 integrity manifest is provided to support verification of authorised copies. Consequently, complete reproduction of text-dependent experiments requires access to the original datasets and the frozen intervention texts. The public archive supports inspection of the methodology and reproduction of analyses for which the necessary inputs or saved instance-level outputs are included. Scope and limitations The reported intervention experiments did not execute pretrained DistilBERT, RoBERTa or DeBERTa baselines. Independent clinical semantic-equivalence adjudication of the generated transformations was not completed. The results are computational and do not establish clinical deployment performance. This record accompanies the associated research manuscript and is intended to support transparent reporting, methodological scrutiny and further replication.

items.summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.

items.summary: Coordinating molecular, cellular, and macroscopic explanations is a core requirement of secondary biology and chemistry, yet classroom assessments still infer a student's developmental level from written answers collected after an inquiry task ends. Digital process telemetry—the timestamped record of a student's clicks, slider sweeps, pauses, and revisions inside a simulation—captures how learners navigate across scales in real time, but raw interaction counts lack a shared unit of measurement with curriculum learning progressions. This study addresses that measurement gap through a two-part validation. First, a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of 86 studies (312 effect sizes; 48,920 learners) synthesized cross-scale inquiry interventions and yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 0.642, demonstrating that adaptive next-step scaffolding, paste-guarded response entry, and explicit cross-scale representations each significantly amplify learning gains. Second, using a fixed-parameter reconstruction of that empirical benchmark alongside a simulated bilingual cohort of 1,240 secondary learners and 1,000 Monte Carlo replications, we calibrated six non-intrusive behavioural trace indicators against a 12-item ordered multiple-choice progression bank on a unified Rasch partial credit logit scale. Common-scale linking error was 0.118 logits (10.9% of the critical Level 2–3 transition interval). Trace-based classifications reproduced item-based progression levels with 81.45% accuracy and Gwet's first-order agreement coefficient of .768, exhibited strict measurement invariance across language tracks, gender, and prior achievement, and confirmed that genuine self-regulatory behaviours rather than interface guardrails drive diagnostic classification. Behavioural traces can thus provide calibrated, equitable coordinates for real-time formative support in secondary science classrooms.

Organizations increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve strategic planning, operational efficiency, and sustainability. However, conventional machine learning models often lack transparency, limiting managerial trust, accountability, and the practical adoption of AI-driven decisions. This study proposes an explainable AI (XAI) framework that integrates predictive analytics, interpretable machine learning, and sustainability indicators to support transparent, reliable, and evidence-based decision-making across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions. The proposed framework combines Random Forest, XGBoost, and Explainable Boosting Machines with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). Evaluation uses a benchmark dataset containing operational performance, resource consumption, organizational efficiency, and environmental indicators. Comparative experiments assess predictive accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), explanation consistency, decision latency, computational cost, and sustainability performance. Baseline models include Logistic Regression, conventional Random Forest, and XGBoost without explanation mechanisms. Ablation studies examine the individual contributions of interpretability and sustainability-aware optimization. The experimental evaluation is designed to determine whether the proposed framework improves predictive reliability, explanation quality, and sustainability-aware decisions compared with conventional approaches. Quantitative reporting will include percentage improvements in predictive performance, reductions in decision latency and resource consumption, and explanation stability across repeated experiments. Qualitative analysis will assess managerial understandability, perceived trustworthiness, fairness, and practical implementation challenges. Numerical outcomes will be reported only after experiments are completed, avoiding unsupported performance claims. The proposed framework establishes a comparative approach for integrating explainability, predictive intelligence, and sustainability into organizational decision-making. By connecting model predictions with transparent explanations and measurable sustainability indicators, the framework aims to strengthen accountability, operational effectiveness, and responsible technology adoption. Future validation across multiple industries will establish its generalizability and practical value.

Qualitative analysis will assess managerial understandability, perceived trustworthiness, fairness, and practical implementation challenges. Numerical outcomes will be reported only after experiments are completed, avoiding unsupported performance claims. The proposed framework establishes a comparative approach for integrating explainability, predictive intelligence, and sustainability into organizational decision-making. By connecting model predictions with transparent explanations and measurable sustainability indicators, the framework aims to strengthen accountability, operational effectiveness, and responsible technology adoption. Future validation across multiple industries will establish its generalizability and practical value.

items.summary: This repository contains supporting materials for the revision of Frontiers in Digital Health manuscript 1986016, examining prior-window home bioimpedance variability and subsequent affected-to-unaffected arm ECW/TBW ratio excursions. The package includes aggregate statistical outputs from the revised analyses, portable Python analysis scripts, a fully synthetic example dataset, variable definitions, analysis provenance, and validation documentation. The supporting materials cover within- and between-participant analyses, observation-weight diagnostics, nonlinear analyses, calendar-time sensitivity analyses, and model convergence assessments. Version 3 update: This version adds materials prepared in response to the subsequent minor-revision review. The new materials include the corrected unaffected-arm comparator using working-independence logistic generalized estimating equations with participant-cluster robust sandwich covariance, the exact-timestamp deduplication and acquisition-time ordering audit, and additional numerical-stability and convergence documentation. Actual participant-level longitudinal measurements, clinical records, identifiers, and ultrasound images are not included because of privacy and ethical restrictions. The synthetic dataset demonstrates the analysis workflow; it does not represent study participants or reproduce the observed study estimates. Exact recomputation of the observed analyses requires authorized access to the restricted source data. These materials supplement the parent-study materials available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22934011 . The manuscript is currently under revision and has not been accepted or published.

items.summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance.
